title: Forum MGP 2026 GS2 Consolidated Questions and Answers

questions.questionText: “The Indian Constitution is merely an amended version of Government of India Act 1935”. Do you  agree? Justify your answer.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.questionText: Explain the concept of residuary powers under the Indian Constitution. Why were they vested in the  Parliament?
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by explaining briefly the concept of residuary powers.
• Next, bring out the reasons for granting the residuary powers to the Centre.
• Conclude by highlighting the judicial position and the recommendations of relevant commissions on the issue. | | --- | **Residuary powers** under the Indian Constitution refer to the **legislative authority** over **matters/subjects** which are **not explicitly enumerated in any of the three lists** (Union List, State List and the Concurrent List). **Article 248 of** the Indian Constitution read with **Entry 97** of **Union** **List**, **vests** the residuary powers exclusively **with the Parliament**. Following are the reasons for vesting **residuary powers in the parliament**: 1. **Post-independence circumstances** (partition, integration of princely states) necessitated the creation of a **strong Centre** for **national unity** and **integrity** (federal system with a unitary bias**)**. 2. Allows a **comprehensive and unified national response** to **evolving needs of governance** and managing **newer issues** whose emergence **could not be foreseen** by the makers of the Constitution (e-Commerce, regulation of IT, AI, blockchain technology). 3. Prevents **legal vacuum** in the absence of state legislation on subjects of critical national importance (Disaster Management, Climate Change, Space Technology). 4. Helps avoid **competitive state legislations on residuary taxes** that may be harmful for balanced national economic development. 5. **Exhaustive nature of the lists** ensured that matters of residuary nature were **expected to be limited** **in number**. As a result, the **allocation of residuary powers to the parliament** was rendered a mere **formality**. Various judicial pronouncements (***Dhillon (1971), Sat Pal (1979)***) and **practical experience** have resulted in an expansion of residuary powers of the legislation in the favour of the Centre. It has also contributed to the federation to be **held together.** Nevertheless, the **Sarkaria Commission, Justice Venkatachaliah** **Commission and Justice Punchhi Commission** have recommended transfer of **residuary powers to the** **Concurrent List,** excluding those related to taxation. (***251 words***)

questions.questionText: Under what circumstances can the Financial Emergency be imposed by the President? What  consequences follow when such a declaration remains in force?
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by briefly outlining the constitutional provisions related to Financial Emergency and highlight the circumstances under which a financial emergency can be imposed by the President.
• Next, bring out the consequences that follow when such a declaration remains in force.
• Conclude by emphasizing the significance of the provisions for Financial Emergency. | | --- | **Article 360** of the Constitution allows the **President to declare** a financial emergency under those circumstances wherein there is a **threat** to the **financial stability or credit of India** or **any part of its territory**. The President must make such a decision based on the **advice of the** **Council of Ministers**. Imposition of a Financial Emergency has **far-reaching consequences** such as: 1. **Dilution of state autonomy** in financial matters; the Union executive can **direct any state** to observe the “**canons of financial propriety”** (set of principles that guide the use of public funds). 2. It empowers the President to issue necessary and adequate directions to **resolve the crisis** (Article 360 (3)). The directions may relate to enforcement of **austerity measures** including provisions for **reducing the salaries and allowances** of state officials. 3. Also, a direction may be issued to the effect that all **money bills** and **financial bills** (under Article 207) passed by the **state legislature** could be required to be reserved for the **consideration of the** **President** (Article 360 4(a)). 4. a) The President may also issue proclamations for similar measures at the **Union level (**reducing the salaries and allowances of officials); b) extension of executive control over **judicial expenses (**salaries and allowances of the members of higher judiciary). Financial Emergency has **never been imposed in the history of independent Indi**a despite occasions that may have warranted its use (1991 financial crisis, COVID-19). Despite criticisms about the **over-centralization** that Financial Emergency entails, the provisions are significant as they allow the Union to **ward-off any threats to** **India’s sovereignty** from economic factors and help preserve the constitutional order. (***264 words***)

questions.questionText: While the Indian Constitution incorporates the principle of separation of powers, it is not 'water-tight'  and is based on the principle of 'checks and balances.' Elucidate.
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • In the Introduction explain the doctrine of separation of power.
• In the body, discuss the separation of powers in the Indian constitution and discuss the functional overlapping of powers.
• Then bring out the principles of checks and balances in the constitution.
• In the conclusion, highlight exclusive and overlapping powers and functions of three organs of government. | | --- | **Separation of powers** is a doctrine of constitutional law given by **Montesquieu**. It provides **distinct functions** **and powers to each branch of the government** to prevent despotism by any single organ and **maintain rule of** **law**. However, the Indian political system does not follow strict separation of power. **In Indian Constitution,** separation of powers is reflected in the following provisions: **1.** The State shall take steps to **separate judiciary from executive** **(Article 50).** **2.** a) Validity of **proceedings in parliament and the legislatures** cannot be called into question in any court (Article 122 and 212); b) judicial **conduct of judges** of supreme court and high courts cannot be discussed in the parliament, except during the process of removal of judges **(Article 121 and 211).** **3.** The **President and Governor are not answerable** to any court for the exercise and performance of powers and duties in their office (**Article 361).** However**, functional overlap between various organs** is also evident: 1. **Legislature exercises judicial and quasi- judicial powers** in case of breach of privileges, disqualifying its members, impeachment of President, removal of judges, amending a law declared ultra vires by the court and revalidating it. **2.** a) Promulgation of ordinances** (Article 123/213); **Ministers** are members of legislature***;*** **appointments** **of judges** of Supreme Court and High Courts by the President***;* b) **bureaucracy** frames rules **(delegated legislation);** c) Tribunals (Article 323A/B)** exercise **judicial powers.**** Also, there is system of **‘checks and balances’** to prevent **‘arbitrary use of power’**: **1.** Supreme Court and High court judges are appointed by the executive. But they can be **removed only** **after an address by Parliament for the same** has been presented to the President. 2. **Legislature holds Executive accountable** through mechanisms like **No Confidence motion,** **Parliamentary Committees,** etc. **3.** **Judiciary keeps a ‘check’** on laws and executive actions so as they conform to the constitutional provisions through **judicial review, Article 142,** etc**.** Thus, separation of power in the Indian political system is **'not water-tight**' but rather based on the principle of **'checks and balances'** where the three organs of government have both **exclusive and overlapping** powers and functions. ***(324 words)***

questions.questionText: What are the essential conditions for the exercise of the legislative powers by the President? Also  discuss the legality of re-promulgation of ordinances without legislative scrutiny.
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief background of the legislative powers of the President.
• In the body, first enumerate the essential conditions for the exercise of the same.
• Next, discuss the legality of the re-promulgation of ordinances by her without placing them before the Parliament.
• Conclude by underlining the significance of the power and the need for constitutional guardrails to prevent its misuse. | | --- | **Part V Chapter III** of the Constitution deals with the **legislative powers of the President of India**. Under **Article** **123**, the **President can promulgate** ordinances when **Parliament is not in session**, ensuring l**egislative** **continuity** in urgent situations. However, the following **essential conditions** need to be fulfilled for the President to exercise this power: 1. An ordinance can be promulgated only when **either one of the two Houses of the Parliament is not** **in session.** 2. Before the promulgation, the President must be satisfied that **urgent circumstances** necessitate **immediate action**. 3. The ordinance must be **approved by Parliament within six weeks** from the date of their reassembly or else it **ceases to be operational** (unless disapproved earlier by a resolution of the Parliament). 4. The President must act on the **aid and advice of the Union Council of Ministers** in promulgating an ordinance and has **no discretion** of her own. 5. The Legislative competence of the President in promulgating an ordinance is restricted to the **subjects** **over which Parliament has jurisdiction** (Union List and Concurrent List). 6. **Constitutional Amendments cannot** be enacted through the ordinance route. There has been significant **debate** regarding the Ordinance making power of the President, particularly with regards to the **legality of re-promulgation of ordinances** without subjecting them to legislative approval: 1. In ***DC Wadhwa (1987),*** it was held that the power of the executive to issue **ordinances** is meant to be used in **exceptional circumstances** and **cannot be a substitute** for a legislative enactment on the subject; the courts were empowered to **strike down re-promulgated ordinances** in order to avoid an **‘Ordinance Raj.’** 2. In ***Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)***, it was held that **re-promulgation** of ordinances without subjecting them to legislative scrutiny is a serious **constitutional infraction** and an **abuse of the constitutional** **process**; it amounts to a “**fraud on power**” and is “**destructive of the rule of law**.” The judgements indicate that while the executive may have **followed the legality and ensured governance** **continuity**, unchecked re-promulgation violates the norms of **constitutional mortality** (Bihar during 1967– 1981). **Mandatory legislative scrutiny** is crucial to prevent **executive overreach.** *(****423 words****)*

questions.questionText: While the Inter-State Council holds considerable potential for addressing federal disputes, this  potential remains largely unrealized. Analyze.
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by briefly elaborating on the constitutional status of the Inter-State Council.
• In the body, first highlight its potential for addressing federal disputes.
• Next, bring out the reasons for non-realization of this potential.
• Lastly, provide suggestions to improve its effectiveness.
• Conclude with the need for concerted efforts from all stakeholders to make Indian federalism more cooperative. | | --- | **Article 263** of the Indian constitution empowers the **President** to establish the **Inter-State Council (ISC)** if it is deemed necessary for **public interest.** Based on the **recommendations of Sarkaria commission** the council was formally constituted in **1990** through a **Presidential order.** Its primary purpose is to **promote cooperation** **and coordination** between the **Centre and the States** and resolve any **disputes** that may arise in India’s federal set-up. The ISC has significant **potential for resolving federal disputes** as: 1. a) Acting as a **platform for dialogue**, ISC helps in finding **common ground**, and fostering **consensus** among the parties involved. b) It encourages cooperative solutions to federal disputes. 2. The Council can give **recommendations to the Centre and states** on matters of common interest, such as policy coordination, boundary disputes, etc. 3. The council (through its standing committee) **monitors the implementation** of its own recommendations as well as those of the **Sarkaria commission** on Centre-state relations. The **challenges** associated with ISC are: 1. a) Its **recommendations are not binding** on the Central or state governments which **limits the** **effectiveness** of the process; b) lack of **political will** undermines the role of ISC as a platform for resolving federal disputes. E.g., ISC did not convene between 2006-2016. 2. a) Different political parties** have divergent interests, and the **short-term electoral priorities** complicate the resolution process making it challenging to achieve consensus;** b) due to **politicization** **of federal issues,** cooperation becomes unviable (alleged discrimination in distribution of Central funds); c) emergence of **specialized forums** like the **GST Council** (for taxation) and NITI Aayog (for policy coordination) **diminishes the scope** of the Council. Following **suggestions** can help improve the role of ISC: 1. a) Reinforcing **the permanent nature of the ISC**, e.g., Council meetings must happen at least twice a year (Punchhi Commission); b) The **recommendations** of ISC can be made **binding** through a constitutional amendment; c) Functional **interlinkages with other interstate bodies** (GST council, NITI Ayog) to improve the political stature of ISC. 2. a) Working of the ISC must be **depoliticized,** so that political parties rise above narrow political interests, e.g., through **rotational chairing** of ISC’s Standing Committee by leaders from states; b) Bureaucratic discussions on policies must be invested with measures for **on-time resolution and** **implementation on ground**, e.g., tabling of reports in the ISC sessions. Enhancing the **Council's role,** providing it with more **resources,** ensuring a **time-bound resolution** process, and encouraging a **cooperative mindset** among all stakeholders can contribute to effective dispute resolution within the **cooperative federalism** framework in India***. (386 words)***

questions.questionText: Describe the appointment process, duties, and functions of the Attorney General of India. Also, state  the restrictions governing the functioning of the office.
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief background about the post of Attorney General of India.
• In the body, describe the appointment process, duties and functions of the Attorney General of India.
• Next, state the restricting governing the functioning of the office.
• Conclude the answer by impressing on the fact that despite being a part of the Union Executive, the Attorney General is not a government servant. | | --- | **Article 76** of the Constitution creates the **office of Attorney General for India**, who is the **highest law officer** in the country. **Appointed by the President,** the AGI must be **qualified to become a judge of the Supreme** **Court**. She holds office **during the pleasure of the President.** As a **convention**, AGI **submits her resignation** **to the President** upon the **change of government**. As the **chief law officer of the Government of India,** the Attorney General has been assigned the following **duties and functions**: 1. a) Advise the government** on **legal matters** referred by the **President (**advice on grant of full GST compensation to states). Performs **duties of a legal character** that are assigned to her by the **President.**** 2. a) Appear **on behalf of the Union Government** in all cases in the **Supreme Court** where the Government of India is a party (e.g., ***Anuradha Bhasin case 2020***); b) represent the Union Government in **High Courts,** when required. 3. a) Represents the Government of India in **any reference** made by the **President** to the **Supreme Court** under **Article 143 (**Presidential reference in 2G case); b) discharge the **functions** conferred on her by the **Constitution or any law (**Contempt of Courts Act 1971). 4. a) Participate in parliamentary proceedings** as and when required, without any **voting rights; b) **assist the Court** in the interest of **rightful administration of justice (**Taj Corridor case). However, certain **limitations** have been placed in the office: 1. a) The Attorney General is **disallowed** to advise or argue **cases against the Union Government;** b) she must not **advise or argue** in cases where she is supposed to advise **for the Union Government.** 2. a) She must not **defend accused persons in criminal proceedings** without the **permission of the** **Union Government;** b) to prevent **conflict of interests,** she must not accept **appointment as a** **director in any company** without government permission. 3. a) The Attorney General must refrain from **advising any government body** unless the **proposal** or a reference in this regard is **received through the Ministry of Law and Justice**. Despite being a **member of the Union Executive,** the Attorney General of India **does not fall** under the category of **government servants.** As a result, **neither** is she a **full-time legal counsel** for the Union Government **nor** is she **debarred from private practice.** ***(351 words)*** **Q.****2) Reorganization of States remains a parliamentary prerogative in India, with the Constitution assigning** **only a consultative role to State legislatures. Examine.** ***Approach: Introduce the answer with articles of the Constitution dealing with reorganization of states. In*** ***the body of answer, examine the factors due to which the reorganization of states remains a parliamentary*** ***prerogative in India, with the Constitution assigning only a consultative role to the State legislatures.*** ***Conclude by highlighting the constitutional safeguards in place to protect the interests of the state.*** **Article 2** of the Constitution deals with **admission or establishment of new states** while **Article 3** deals **with** **alteration** of areas, **boundaries or names** of existing states. These provisions establish India as an **indestructible union of destructible states**, a feature of **federal state** with **unitary bias.** While the **Constitution provides substantial power to State Assemblies**, reorganization of states remains a parliamentary prerogative in India. The State legislatures have been assigned only a consultative role in the process due to the following factors: 1. While the **drafting of the Constitution**, India was emerging from colonial **rule.** Given the challenges of a **nascent democracy** and the **recent partition**, constitution-makers favoured **centralized control** over **state reorganization.** They believed it was crucial to prevent **balkanization** and preserve the unity **and integrity** of India. 2. After independence, **existing boundaries** were seen as **arbitrary remnants of colonial rule**. **Redrawing boundaries** was recognized as **necessary** due to this reason. However, involving the states directly risked **prioritizing regional over national interests**. Parliamentary control ensured balanced decision-making for **national cohesion and stability.** E.g., Patiala and East Punjab States Union **(PEPSU) merged into Punjab** state in 1956. 3. **Administrative convenience** and **practicality** were also important considerations. Parliamentary control over the matter ensures a **standardized process** across the country. It provides **consistency** in dealing with **demands for new states or** alterations in state boundaries. Also, **regional aspirations** have been **accommodated by the Parliament** from time to time. E.g., reorganization of NE states, creation of **Telangana (2014)**. Nevertheless, the framers of the Constitution put **safeguards in place** to protect the interest of the **affected** **states**. Any bill for the reorganisation of the states requires **prior recommendation** of the President. The concerned State Assembly has to be **consulted** by the President and the bill must also be **scrutinized and passed** by the **Council of States**.***(297 words)***

questions.questionText: “Structural weaknesses and implementation challenges continue to undermine the effectiveness of  the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution”. Comment.
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief background of the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution.
• In the body, first highlight its successes.
• Next, point out how structural weaknesses and implementation challenges continue to undermine its effectiveness.
• the ways in which it has failed to achieve its objectives.
• Conclude with suggestions to reform the law. | | --- | **Tenth Schedule of the Constitution**, also known as the **anti-defection law**, was inserted via the **52****nd** **Constitutional Amendment (1985).** It contains provisions to **disqualify legislators** from their membership on **grounds of defection**. It has played an important role in **safeguarding the foundations of democracy** in the following ways: 1. The law has **strengthened democratic stability** by reducing **individual defections**. This has led to stable governments and **fewer premature elections** at both central and state levels. 2. The disqualification provision **bars the defectors** from **ministerial positions**. This has effectively reduced **opportunistic party-switching**(Aaya Ram Gaya Ram) driven by the **'lure of office’.** 3. The legislation has improved **party discipline** and **organizational cohesion** through strong **disincentives** against **arbitrary defections**. 4. Ensured respect for **popular mandate** which is often linked to a candidate’s **party affiliation** or **independent status.** 5. The **constitutional framework** established by the law provides a **clear mechanism (**e.g. grounds and procedure for disqualification) for addressing political defections. Despite these positive outcomes, **structural weaknesses** and **implementation challenges** continue to **undermine the law's effectiveness**, as highlighted in the Law Commission's 170th report: 1. a) **Loopholes** in the law (disqualification ceases to be effective on re-election) have been **exploited** to **manufacture mass resignations** (Karnataka) and **destabilize governments** (Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand); b) defections have been engineered to **deplete the ranks** of Opposition in the legislature (West Bengal). 2. **Practical challenges** have arisen because of the **Speaker's role** as the **adjudicating authority**. Courts have raised question marks on the **neutrality of the Speaker** (*Keisham Meghchandra Singh* *case 2020*) and **delays in deciding** disqualification petitions (*Maharashtra Speaker case 2020*). 3. a) **Exemption** granted to **merger** of 2/3rd members has been maneuvered to **serve political interests** (Goa); b) The law does not cover **activities outside** the legislature which are contrary to the **spirit of** **the law** (Jignesh Mevani case 2022). 4. a) Party leadership** has been **disproportionately strengthened** through the power to issue **whips**. This has come at the cost of **autonomy** of individual legislators (restricted freedom of speech and conscience) and **intra-party democracy** (can be used to curb dissent);** b) **ambiguous phrases** (“voluntarily gives up membership”) have resulted in **inconsistent interpretation** and **application**. The recommendations of the Halim Committee, NCRWC, and Supreme Court judgments calling for **independent tribunals** and **fixed timelines for decisions** provide a **roadmap for reform**. These **institutional** **changes**, coupled with strengthening **intra-party democracy**, would help realize the **law's original objectives**. (***388 words***) **Q.4)** **While tribunals have their salience in the Indian justice system, they are beset with multiple** **challenges. Elaborate**. ***Approach: Introduce by writing about tribunals and relevant Articles of Constitution. In the body, first*** ***discuss their salience in the Indian justice system. In the next part, mention the multiple challenges they*** ***are beset with. Conclude by highlighting recent developments in the direction of improving their*** ***effectiveness.*** Tribunals are **quasi-judicial bodies** established to adjudicate specific **administrative matters** outlined in **Article 323A**, or **other designated areas (**e.g. taxation, industrial disputes) as specified in **Article 323B.** Tribunals have great **salience** in the Indian justice system, as discussed below: 1. a) Facilitate **speedier disposal** of cases (informal procedures- e.g. guided by principles of natural justice), thereby helping reduce **judicial backlog** (e.g. CAT); b) non-adversarial nature of proceedings** enables more consensual disposal of complicated cases (e.g. NCLT).** 2. a) Bring **domain knowledge** through integration of domain experts, thereby enabling **specialized** **adjudication** (e.g. ITAT); b) provide avenues for **low-cost litigation,** especially to the weaker sections of the society (e.g. Maintenance Tribunals under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007). 3. a) Enhance **access to justice** in far-fetched corners of the country (e.g. through regional benches); b) pioneer **progressive jurisprudence** in emerging areas (e.g. environmental justice- NGT) However, tribunals’ functioning is **beset with multiple challenges:** 1. a) **Executive interference** in functioning (e.g. in appointment of chairpersons/members) violates the principle of **separation of powers;** b) **structural issues** with the tribunals (vacancies, inadequate support staff, infrastructural gaps) reduce their functionality. 2. a) Diversity in **composition, structure and statutes** has created confusion about their powers, jurisdiction and functions, leading to **tribunalization of justice;** b) frequent appeals** against their decisions end up **prolonging** the judicial process, increasing **financial burden** on the parties and causing **judicial delays.**** **Tribunal Reform Act 2021** rationalized the **number of tribunals** to address some of these concerns. However, to ensure these bodies **fulfill their intended mandate**, these reforms must be complemented with the suggestions of the Supreme Court (**judicial impact assessment, National Tribunals Commission)**. ***(302*** ***Words)***

questions.questionText: “The Supreme Court’s recognition of environmental issues within the constitutional framework has  been a landmark transformation in contemporary Indian legal discourse.” Discuss the statement with the  help of relevant case laws.
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief background of the recent Supreme Court judgement on adverse effects of climate change.
• In the body, discuss the role played by the Indian judiciary in constitutionalization of environmental issues, citing relevant case laws.
• Conclude by highlighting the importance of this constitutionalization. | | --- | In a landmark judgment in **M.K. Ranjitsinh vs. Union of India** (April 2024), the Supreme Court recognized the **'right against adverse effects of climate change'** as a **distinct fundamental right** under **Articles 14 and 21** of the Constitution. This judgment represents a **continuation** of decades of judicial interpretation that has **progressively 'constitutionalized'** environmental protection through various **landmark decisions**, as detailed below: 1. **Constitutional interpretation** expanding **Article 21** to include environmental rights: 1.1. a) The Supreme Court in **M.C. Mehta** v. Union of India (1987) established that the right to life includes the **right to a healthy environment.** It also introduced the **doctrine of absolute** **liability**; b) **Subhash Kumar** v. State of Bihar (1991)** recognized that the right to **pollution-** **free water and air** comes within the purview of Article 21.** 1.2. **Virender Gaur** v. State of Haryana (1995) emphasized that **hygienic environment** is an **integral facet** of right to healthy life, while stressing upon State’s fundamental duty to maintain **ecological balance.** 2. **Public trust doctrine** incorporation through judicial pronouncements: 2.1. a) The landmark case of **M.C. Mehta** v. Kamal Nath (1997) established that **natural resources** are **held in trust** by the government for public use; b) **M.I. Builders** v. Radhey Shyam Sahu (1999) applied this doctrine to protect **public parks**; c) **Intellectuals Forum** v. State of AP (2006) extended the doctrine to protect **water bodies** from **encroachment.** 3. **“Precautionary Principle”** and “**Polluter Pays Principle”** integration: 3.1. a) **Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum** v. Union of India (1996) declared these principles as part of **environmental law**; b) **Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action** v. Union of India (1996) applied the polluter pays principle to make **industries liable** for **environmental restoration.** 3.2. **A.P. Pollution Control Board** v. Prof. M.V. Nayudu (1999) established that lack of **scientific** **certainty** cannot justify postponing environmental **protection measures**, placing the **burden** **of proof** on parties proposing potentially **harmful activities** (framework for applying precautionary principle). 4. **Procedural innovations** enhancing environmental justice: 4.1. Expansion of **Public Interest Litigation (PIL)** in environmental matters through cases like **Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra** v. State of UP (1985)** enabling citizens to approach courts for environmental protection.** 4.2. a) Adoption of **continuing mandamus** in T.N. Godavarman v Union of India, allowing courts to **monitor environmental compliance**; b) establishment of **specialized benches** and **National Green Tribunal** through **judicial recommendations** and consequent legislation. (e.g., National Green Tribunal Act, 2010) 5. **Sustainable Development** framework development: 5.1. **T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad** v. Union of India series established a comprehensive **forest** **conservation framework** (e.g., expanded the definition of **'forest' beyond statutory** **boundaries**) 5.2. a) **Narmada Bachao Andolan** v. Union of India (2000) balanced **development needs** with **environmental protection** (explaining the concept of sustainable development); b) **M.C.** **Mehta** v. Union of India (2004) (Delhi CNG case) promoted **sustainable urban transport** systems. This **evolution** of environmental jurisprudence has **operationalized the mandate** of Article 48A, transforming the **Directive Principle** of environmental protection into **concrete mechanisms** for **environmental** **stewardship** and **ecological preservation.** ***(454 words)***

questions.questionText: Explain the structure of the Parliamentary Committee system. How far have the Departmentally  Related Standing Committees (DRSCs) helped in the institutionalisation of Indian Parliament?
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer with a brief background of the Parliamentary Committee system.
• In the body, first explain the structure of the same.
• Next, highlight the extent to which they have helped in the institutionalization of Indian Parliament.
• Conclude by suggesting reforms to improve their functioning. | | --- | Parliamentary Committee is a group of MPs who are **appointed or elected** by the House or **nominated by the** **chairperson of the house.** It studies and deliberates on **a range of subject matters**, Bills, and budgets of the ministries. It works under **the chairperson’s** **direction** and presents its **report to the chairperson or the** **House.** By their nature, Parliamentary Committees are of the following **two kinds**: 1. **Standing Committees**: a) **Permanent and regular committees,** which are **re-constituted from** **time to time;** b) three types of committees come under this category - **Financial Committees (**Public Accounts Committee**), Departmentally related Standing Committees (**Committee on Commerce) and **Other Parliamentary Standing Committees (**Business Advisory Committee). 2. **Ad hoc Committees:** a) Appointed for a **specific purpose** and **cease to exist** when the task is **finished;** b) divided into two categories- **Inquiry Committees (**JPC on 2G spectrum case) and **Advisory Committees (**JPC on Waqf Bill). **Departmentally Related Standing Committees** (DRSCs) cover under their **jurisdiction** all the **Ministries/** **Departments of the Government of India** and comprise **members** from both the **Lok Sabha (21)** and the **Rajya** **Sabha (10).** They have played a crucial role in the **institutionalization of Parliament** in the following ways: 1. a) Consider the **demand for grants** of various ministries, thus aiding **effective debate over the** **Budget**; b) **examine** in-depth the **bills** referred to them, analyze **policies** and provide their **suggestions to strengthen** the same. 2. a) Provisions of **anti-defection laws** are **not applicable** to Committee proceedings. This allows individual **MPs to freely voice their opinions**; b) **closed-door nature of proceedings** enables members to **diverge from party line** and r**each consensus** on critical matters. 3. a) Provide a platform for **domain experts** to consult with public representatives and provide their inputs in policy making; b) reflect the principles of **direct democracy** by engaging with **grassroots** **organizations, civil society groups** and the **general public**. 4. a) Help make up for the l**oss of time** (disruptions, adjournments) on the **floor of the House**; b) **continuous nature of the functioning** of Committees compensates for the **steady decline in the** **sittings of the Parliament** (average annual sitting of the 17th Lok Sabha-55 days). 5. a) Enable the **Rajya Sabha** in exercising **financial control** over the Executive indirectly; b) facilitate **intellectual development of individual MPs** who can focus on particular policy domains and build expertise therein; c) make space for **opposition** to contribute to **government functioning**. However, the following **factors** have impeded the ability of the DRSCs in this regard: 1. a) **Decrease** in the number of bills being referred to the Committees (only 16% in the 17th Lok Sabha); b) **non-binding** nature of the **recommendations** of the Committee. 2. a) Decline** in the working of the Committees (delays in submitting reports, lesser number of sittings for specific bills, lower attendance of members);** b) growing instances of **divisions along partisan lines** in Committee proceedings (Data Protection Bill, Waqf Bill). 3. a) Handicaps in functioning due to **absence** of **standing research support** (highlighted by NCRWC); b) non-consideration of **members’ own expertise** while nominating them to different committees. This, coupled with **short tenure** (1 year), leads to **ad-hocism** in their functioning. The DRSC System is a path-breaking endeavour of **parliamentary surveillance over administration**. There is a need to improve the functioning of these **“mini-Parliaments”** through sustained **secretarial and research** **support**. This will allow them to better **guide the Executive** in the achievement of **long-term national goals**. (***404 words***)

questions.questionText: Critically discuss the need for the codification of parliamentary privileges in the country.
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by highlighting the different sources of parliamentary privileges and the absence of a definitive Code for the same.
• In the body, discuss the need for the codification of parliamentary privileges in the country, highlighting both the positives and negatives of the same.
• Conclude by underlining the need to incorporate international best practices in the exercise of privileges. | | --- | **Article 105 (3)** empowers **Parliament to define the Parliamentary Privileges**. However, in the **absence of** **such a law**, parliamentary privileges continue to be derived from diverse **sources**-**Constitution, statutes,** **judicial interpretation, rules of procedure** and established **conventions**. Several experts have flagged the **ambiguity** and **the potential for their misuse** in the absence of a definitive Code of Parliamentary privileges. They have argued in **favour of such a code on account** of the following reasons: 1. The present system **equates Indian Parliament** and **British House of Commons** (despite the reference to Section 15 of 44th Amendment). While the latter is regarded as **sovereign**, the former is subject to **constitutional limitations**. A Code of Parliamentary Privileges will **uphold the supremacy** **of the Constitution** as opposed to the supremacy of Parliament. 2. a) Codification can **remove the uncertainty in their application**. This uncertainty creates **potential** **for misuse** by curbing the **freedom of speech** of the citizens (Karnataka Assembly case 2017); b) It can strengthen the **right of information** of the citizens (definitive guidelines to prevent arbitrary redaction of parliamentary proceedings); c) such a system will uphold the ideals of **constitutionalism** (limited power). 3. a) A codified framework can also provide **safeguards against attempts to stifle dissent** or suppress **minority voices** within the legislature. Protecting the **rights of individual parliamentarians** can strengthen the democratic principles of representation and pluralism; b) Clear guidelines and mechanisms would demonstrate the **commitment of the legislature to transparency and fairness**. 4. a) It will delineate the limits and conditions under which privileges can be invoked. This can help prevent the use of privileges as a **shield** to protect MPs from **legitimate scrutiny.** b) such codification will allow the **judiciary to examine the validity of privilege claims** and preserve the constitutional principle of **checks and balances**. Despite the aforementioned advantages of codification, lawmakers have put forward the following **reasons in** **opposition to codification:** 1. a) Codification of privileges is likely to have adverse consequences for the **independence of the** **Parliament** and **separation of powers**; b) any law enacted for codification will be **subject to judicial** **scrutiny** for inconsistency with the **Fundamental Rights** (Patna Searchlight Case). 2. a) Any legislation aimed at codification will be a reflection of the **will of the current Executive** which holds majority. Such a law may curtail the **privileges of Opposition members**; b) crystallization of privileges in a code may **reduce the interpretive power of the Presiding officers.** This will impact their ability to respond to **practical challenges in the functioning** of the House. Several **other democratic countries such as Australia** have taken concrete steps in the direction of **codification of Parliamentary privileges.** Until such time as codification takes place, **India can incorporate** **best practices** from other countries. This will help ensure that **safeguarding Parliamentary privileges** does not conflict with **rights of citizens and accountability of members**. (***453 words***)

questions.questionText: Explain and distinguish between the Finance Commission of India and the GST Council. Do their  overlapping jurisdictions create challenges in fiscal governance?
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by briefly explaining about the Finance Commission and GST Council.
• In the body, bring out the differences between the two bodies.
• Next, answer whether their overlapping jurisdictions create challenges in fiscal governance.
• Conclude by highlighting the need for coordination between them. | | --- | **Finance Commission** is a **constitutional body** set up under **Article 280**. It is constituted primarily to determine the **principles of distribution of revenues** between Centre and states and among the states. The **GST Council** is a **constitutional body** set up under **Article 279A** in pursuance of the **101****st** **Constitution Amendment Act** **201**6. It has been entrusted with the task of **making recommendations related to GST to the Union and** **states**. Following are the **differences** between the two bodies: **Finance Commission** **GST Council** 1. a) Present in the **original Constitution**; b) **non-**1. a) Added by the **101****st** **Amendment** to the **permanent body** usually set up **every 5 years** by Constitution; b) **permanent body** set up by the President. the President in 2016. 2. a) Membership** comprises **non-official experts** 2.** a) Elected representatives** (Ministers in in **public affairs, financial administration** etc, Union and State governments) are **ex-officio** making it a **technocratic body**;** b) qualifications of **members,** which make it a **political body**; b) members **determined** **by** **law** (Finance membership is **provided** **for** **in** **the** Commission Act 1951). **Constitution** itself. 3. a) Makes **recommendations** related to **revenue** 3. a) Makes **recommendations** **regarding** **sharing, inter-governmental fiscal relations,** **issues related to the GST framework** (rates, **fiscal discipline** etc, covering a **wider ambit of** exemptions, norms of compliance); **fiscal matters**. recommendations cover **only a specific field** of fiscal landscape. Their **overlapping jurisdictions** create the following **challenges in fiscal governance**: 1. GST **Council's decisions** (rates, exemptions, and compensation) **directly impact** the **divisible pool** (CGST) calculated by the Finance Commission, creating **revenue distribution tensions** that undermine constitutional devolution frameworks. 2. Finance Commission's **medium-term fiscal roadmap** faces disruption from GST Council's **frequent** **policy adjustments**, resulting in **coordination gaps** and **temporal misalignments** that complicate **revenue forecasting** e.g., GST compensation shortfalls sparked Centre-state conflicts during COVID- 19. 3. The **GST Council's structure** with Union government's **effective veto power** creates **asymmetric** **influence** in **fiscal federalism** compared to the Finance Commission's **independent constitutional** **operation**. As a matter of prudence, it is important to put in place a **co-ordination mechanism between the GST Council** **and the Finance Commission** to eliminate **information gaps** between them. It will help them realize their true potential as **important cogs** in the **wheels of fiscal federalism.** **(412 words)**

questions.questionText: “Granting statutory backing to the Model Code of Conduct (MCC) shall empower the Election  Commission of India (ECI) with the much-needed legal authority to conduct free and fair elections.”  Comment.
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief account of the Model Code of Conduct (MCC) and highlight recent instances of its breach.
• In the body, first mention the arguments in favour of giving statutory backing to MCC.
• Next, discuss challenges it may entail.
• Conclude with suggesting a way forward. | | --- | The Model Code of Conduct (MCC) is a **set of guidelines** published by the Election Commission of India **(ECI)** for political parties and candidates to set **standards of conduct** during the election campaign and polling. However, the **effectiveness** of these guidelines is being increasingly **called into question** due to **recurrent** **violations** (>1000 violations during Delhi elections 2025), including by **high constitutional authorities** (Azam Khan case). As a result, some experts have suggested granting **MCC statutory status** to strengthen the **ECI’s enforcement** **powers** to conduct free and fair elections in the following ways: 1. a) ECI will have **greater authority** to **penalize violations**; b) **legal consequences** rather than mere reprimands will **deter** **non-compliance.** 2. Use of **ECI’s plenary power** to enforce the MCC may **possibly encroach** on **Parliament’s** **jurisdiction**. A law is likely to avoid this through **definitive provisions**. 3. It can resolve the absence of **immediate grievance redressal** mechanisms for any concerns of stakeholders in the election process (cancellation of nomination). **Presently,** the decision can only be challenged in the **High Court** after the announcements of results. 4. It would ensure a **uniform application** of the MCC, **eliminating inconsistencies** in its enforcement. However, other stakeholders, including the ECI have **opposed providing statutory backing** to the MCC for the following reasons: 1. a) Elections are completed in a relatively **short time** and **judicial proceedings** are longer; b) a law will replace the **summary procedure** for **prompt action** with a lengthy judicial procedure. c) judicial interventions may **complicate the managemen**t of the election process by exposing it to **excessive** **litigation**. 2. a) Statutorization would entail **enhancing administrative capacity** of ECI to handle the **increased** **responsibilities** and **legal processes;** b) political parties may **resist** statutory backing, perceiving it as a **constraint** on their campaign activities. 3. a) Many provisions of the MCC are **already enforceable** through other legislations like RPA and IPC (violation of secrecy of voting, causing enmity among communities). b) The broad objectives of MCC are best achieved by **voluntary compliance** and **oversight of an impartial watchdog. Violations** incur **reprimands** from the EC, causing significant **embarrassment** for political actors (media scrutiny, societal backlash). Though MCC has no statutory backing it carries significant **moral weight.** Given the **practical difficulties in** **giving statutory backing** to the MCC, another alternative would be **amending RPA** acts to deal with specific issues of electoral malpractices. (***387 words***)

questions.questionText: What steps are required for the constitutionalization of a Commission? Do you think granting  constitutional status to the Central Information Commission (CIC) would strengthen the RTI regime in  India? Give reasons.
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Give an introduction explaining the term constitutionalization.
• In the body, first list the steps needed for constitutionalization of a commission.
• Next, discuss the ways in which constitutionalization of the Central Information Commission could strengthen the RTI regime.
• Lastly, bring out the challenges of constitutionalization.
• Conclude by highlighting the need to take other measures to strengthen the RTI regime. | | --- | **Constitutionalization** of a body refers to the process of **incorporating provisions** related to its composition, functions, and powers directly into a **country's Constitution**, thereby elevating its **legal status** and **institutional significance**. The process would require an **amendmen**t to the Constitution under **Article 368** and can be done in following **steps**: 1. Introduction of a **Constitution Amendment Bill** in either House detailing the **commission’s** **composition, mandate, powers,** jurisdiction, etc. 2. **Scrutinising and passage** of the bill by **both the Houses** through **special majority** (majority of the total membership and 2/3rd members present and voting). 3. **Ratification** by half of the **State Legislatures** (if affecting the federal provisions) E.g. NJAC 4. **Presidential assent** to the amendment (and consequent publication in the **official** **gazette)** would result in **constitutionalisation** of the commission. 5. For example, in 2018, the National Commission for Backward Classes **(NCBC)** was given **constitutional status** (338B) through the **102nd Amendment Act**. The Central Information Commission (**CIC**) is currently a **statutory body** established under the **Right to** **Information** Act, 2005. Granting it **constitutional status** could **strengthen the RTI regime** in the following ways: 1. Raise its **institutional standing** and **elevate** the CIC's position in the **governance hierarchy**, giving its orders greater **legal weight, strengthen enforcement** of its decisions and improve **compliance by** **public authorities**. 2. Would safeguard the CIC from efforts of **transient legislative majorities** to curb its autonomy (RTI Amendment Act 2019). This will promote l**ong-term continuity of the RTI regime** itself. 3. Constitutional recognition would enhance the **institutional legitimacy of the CIC**, reinforcing **public** **trust** in the RTI framework. This would signal a strong commitment to **transparency, accountability,** and **citizen empowerment** in governance. 4. Granting constitutional status to the CIC can be considered the **next logical step** after the **Right to** **Information** has been judicially recognized as part of **Article 19 and 21**. 5. It may also enable **the CIC with financial and administrative autonomy,** helping address issues such as prolonged **vacancies and funding constraints** and empower it to **address regional disparities** in the implementation of the Act. Constitutionalization, however, is **unlikely to address** the following challenges of the RTI regime: 1. Limited **implementation capacity** in government departments due to **shortage of dedicated** **personnel** (officials often performing **dual roles** as PIOs) and funds. 2. Repeated resort to **Section 8 (1)** of the RTI Act to deny information to citizens; restrictive laws (Official Secrets Act) that promote a general **culture of secrecy** in government functioning. 3. Weaker **whistle-blower protection mechanisms** and challenges of **safety and security of RTI** **activists** (>100 RTI activists killed since 2005). 4. Constitutionalization may introduce an element of **rigidity in the RTI** regime and create potential for **institutional conflict** due to **overlapping jurisdictions.** While granting constitutional status to the **CIC could strengthen its authority**, it is **not a panacea** for all challenges. **Complementary reforms** (increasing capacity of government departments, suo-moto disclosures, operationalising whistleblower protection mechanisms) need to be implemented to **strengthen the RTI regime**. ***(408 words)***

questions.questionText: Describe the functions and powers of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC). Can it  enforce the implementation of constitutional reservations for the Scheduled Castes in religious minority  institutions?
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Give an introduction providing a brief background about the NCSC.
• In the body, first mention its functions and powers, then explain whether it can enforce the implementation of reservations for Scheduled Caste in religious minority institutions.
• Conclude by suggesting a way forward. | | --- | National Commission for Scheduled Castes (NCSC) is a **constitutional** body established under **Article 338** to provide safeguards against the exploitation of **Scheduled Castes** and **Anglo-Indian communities**. It aims to promote and protect their **social, educational, economic,** and **cultural interests**. Under **Article 338 (5),** the Commission is mandated to perform the following functions: 1. a) **Monitor** and **investigate** all issues related to **legal** and **constitutional safeguards** for SCs (Special Report on non-implementation of reservation in BHU-2013); b) **evaluate their working (**Special Report on Reservation in Promotion-2014). 2. Look into specific **complaints** related to the **deprivation of rights and safeguards** (Report on atrocities against Kuravan community in TN-2016) 3. a) Provide **advisory input** in **socio-economic** **development planning** for Scheduled Castes (Report on the Scheduled Castes Sub Plan-2016); b) evaluate their **progress** at both the national and state levels. 4. Prepare and submit **detailed reports** to the President of India regarding the implementation and functioning of constitutional safeguards for Scheduled Castes. 5. a) **Suggest measures** to the **Central** and **State Governments** to enhance the implementation of protective safeguards (Report on plight of Safai Karmacharis-2016); b) propose **broader** **recommendations** for improving the **protection, welfare, and development** of SCs (Special Report on Reservation in judiciary-2013). Moreover, the **President may** ask the Commission **to discharge any other functions** to fulfill its mandate.To effectively carry out its functions, it has been granted the **powers of a civil court** (summoning witness, calling evidence etc). It also has the **power to determine its own procedure** (Article 338(4)). As part of its mandate, the **NCSC** also **oversees** the **implementation of reservation provisions.** However, it **cannot enforce** the implementation of reservation for SCs in the religious minority institutions due to **constitutional exemptions (**Article 15(5)- exempts them from implementing reservations) and **judicial** **pronouncements** ***(Ashok Thakur 2008***). Although it cannot enforce reservations in minority educational institutions, the NCSC can still play a significant role in **ensuring greater educational opportunities** for SC students (through recommendations, scholarships). This will allow it to uphold its constitutional mandate as the **watchdog for the rights and welfare of SCs.** ***(357*** ***words)***

questions.questionText: What factors contributed to the establishment of the National Green Tribunal? To what extent, in  your opinion, has it been successful in fulfilling its intended objectives?
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief background about NGT.
• In the body, first bring out the factors that led to its establishment.
• Next, provide your opinion on the extent of its success in fulfilling its intended objectives.
• Conclude with suggestions for improvement. | | --- | **National Green Tribunal (NGT)** is a **quasi judicial authority** established under **NGT Act, 2010.** It is a **specialized tribunal** to handle **environmental disputes** involving **multi-disciplinary issues**. Its **establishment** was an outcome of the following **factors**: 1. a) Growing **environmental awareness** and the **exponential rise** in environment-related **litigation** necessitated a specialized forum to **prevent overburdening** regular courts; b) the **technical** **complexities** of environmental issues necessitated involving **domain experts** in adjudication (highlighted in *AP Pollution Control Board 1999*). 2. a) **Constitutionalization** of environmental rights expanded the scope of **environmental** **jurisprudence** (right to healthy environment interpreted under Article 21); b) emergence of **multiple** **environmental challenges** (pollution, deforestation) due to **population explosion** and rapid economic development. 3. a) Need for a specialized body to **adjudicate disputes arising from** **statutory frameworks** (EPA 1986, Biodiversity Act 2002); b) major **industrial accidents** spotlighted the need for a body to adjudicate on **damage claims** (Bhopal Gas tragedy case, Oleum Gas Leak case). 4. a) **Poor performance** of bodies like the **NEAA, NET** (186th Law Commission report); requirements stemming from India’s **international commitments** (**Principle 10** of the Rio Earth Summit 1992). NGT has achieved major **successes** in fulfilling its intended objectives. However, several of its **shortcomings** have also come to the fore. The table below highlights both: **Successes** **Shortcomings** 1. a) **Flexibility in procedure** (procedure governed by 1. a) Persistently high pendency** despite good principles of natural justice) allows it to hear cases disposal rate;** b) numerous **vacancies** among on “**environmental merits”** rather than on purely judicial and expert members hamper effective legal merits**;** b) other procedural innovations** ( functioning. **‘ground truthing’,** **zero adjournment policy**) have 2. Concerns over the ‘**lack of environmental** expedited dispute settlement. **finesse**’ among expert members and** 2. a) High rate of disposal** (more cases resolved **economic impact** of its decisions (*Mopa* than instituted during 2018-23);** b) dedicated *Airport Case*). efforts to resolve **complex cases and backlogs**. 3. a) Alleged **over-stepping** of jurisdictional 3. a) Steps to **enhance accessibility** (video-boundaries(suo-moto cognizance, exercising conferencing, letter petitions); b) effective judicial review)and tendency to **expand** its **monitoring of compliance** with SC orders (Ganga authority (*Kalpavriksha case*); b) concerns have rejuvenation). been raised regarding **procedural fairness,** 4. a) Collaboration with government** authorities to particularly in cases where **expert committee** resolve major environmental challenges (**solid** **reports** were accepted without **adequate** **and liquid waste management); b) ensured **consultation** with affected parties. enforcement of **polluter pays principle** (Rs. 20000 4. a) Issues of **accessibility** (zonal benches fine on dumping waste in Hindon canal). located only in five cities); b) differences in **capabilities of regional benches** and principal bench cause **regional** **disparities** **in** **enforcement** of environmental laws. NGT has played a crucial role in **environmental governance.** However, **instituting reforms in the NGT Act** (more regional benches, well-defined jurisdiction) are extremely important for the tribunal to **achieve its** **objectives** and guide India towards **sustainable development**. (***447 words)*** **EPA:** Environment Protection Act; **NEAA:** National Environment Appellate Authority**; NET:** National Environmental Tribunal

questions.questionText: Lateral entry into civil services is seen as a reformative step, yet it continues to attract criticism and  controversy. Discuss.
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by giving a brief background about lateral entry into civil services.
• In the body, first bring out its reformative potential and then highlight the points of criticism and controversy that it attracts.
• Conclude by highlighting the need for accompanying reforms to improve governance. | | --- | Lateral entry refers to **recruiting individuals** from outside the **traditional civil service cadres** to fill **mid and** **senior-level positions** (Joint Secretary, Director) in government departments, typically on a **contractual basis.** They were formally **institutionalised** in 2018. **Executed through the UPSC**, they are seen as a **reformative step** due to the following reasons: 1. **Emerging global polycrisis (**trade wars, climate change**)** will likely cause greater **complexity for** **governance.** Greater engagement of **specialists** and **domain experts** will allow systems to **bridge** **talent gaps** and tackle these challenges effectively. Eg., AI Governance. 2. a) It can bring **performance-driven**, result-oriented leadership to improve delivery systems and can help overcome **bureaucratic inertia**; b) lateral entry could **compensate for staff shortages,** highlighted by the **Baswan Committee (2016)**. 3. a) Can induce a **healthy competition** between lateral entrants and career bureaucrats making governance more **efficient** and **citizen centric**; b) may bring in **work ethics** of the corporate sector (data driven decision making, agile organisation). 4. a) Lateral entrants can bring **innovation** and **new approaches** to governance through an **outsider’s** **perspective;** b) this may help make governance more **participatory** and prevent it from **becoming** **isolated** from the challenges faced by **various stakeholders.** Some experts, however, consider the move as **controversial and criticise** it on the following grounds: 1. a) While career civil servants are **trained within a constitutional framework** of welfarism and equity, lateral entrants from **corporate backgrounds** may sometimes **prioritize short-term goals** over inclusive development; b) may lack the deep **institutional knowledge** and **administrative experience** that career officers acquire. 2. a) **Risk of politicisation** arises if lateral hires are chosen based on **ideological alignment** rather than competence, potentially undermining the civil services’ **neutrality** and **non-partisanship**; b) can generate **conflict of interest**, creating a **revolving door** between the **private sector and government**. 3. a) **Entrenched bureaucratic strongholds,** with their possible **aversion to lateral entry,** may result in new hires encountering some **resistance or non-cooperation** from within departments; b) **cultural** **shock** on shifting from the corporate world to a government department, can **impact work quality.** 4. a) Very **short tenure** of service (just 3 to 5 years), makes it **difficult to measure performance,** **establish responsibility and ensure accountability**; b) **non-application of reservation policy** likely violates the constitutional scheme of things **(**withdrawal of notification for recruitment in August 2024**).** Recommended by the **first ARC** as far back as 1965, lateral entry is an important reform. However, it needs to be complemented with other measures- **merit-based promotions, private sector deputations** etc. This will help realize the motto of ***Yogah Karmasu Kaushala,*** denoting **efficiency in action.** ***(402 words)*** **Additional resources** Lateral Entry into Civil Services- Rationale and Criticisms- Explained pointwise |ForumIAS The need is for domain experts, but within the civil service - The Hindu Lateral entry in UPSC will further distance marginalised from centres of power | The Indian Express

questions.questionText: Public charitable trusts have the potential to make India's development more inclusive as they relate  to certain vital public issues. Comment.
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce by explaining about public charitable trusts.
• In the body, first elaborate upon their role in making India's development more inclusive.
• Next, mention the challenges associated with their functioning.
• Conclude by suggestions to aid the efforts of these trust towards India’s development. | | --- | Public charitable trusts are **non-profit legal entities** established to provide **welfare** to the masses, such as education, healthcare, poverty relief, etc., They are usually governed by **state-specific legislation**, such as The Maharashtra Public Trust Act, 1950. They are mostly funded by **donations** and managed by **trustees.** As organizations working for the **welfare of the community,** they have the potential to make **India’s** **development more inclusive** in the following ways: 1. a) Fill critical **gaps** in **healthcare**, **education**, and **basic services**, especially in rural and remote areas. E.g. Satya Bharti School Programme providing free quality education to underprivileged children**;** b) focus on **marginalized communities** often overlooked by government programs.E.g., works of **Azim** **Premji Foundation** to provide last-mile health services in tribal belts of central India. 2. a) Flexible approach** enables **targeted** **solutions**. E.g., Internet Saathi initiative by the **Tata Trusts** providing digital literacy to rural women;** b) leverage significant **funding** from the private sector and philanthropic organizations. E.g., **Bill and Melinda Gates foundation;** c) implement **innovative** **approaches to public welfare**. E.g., centralized kitchen model of **Akshaya Patra Foundation**. 3. a) Enhance prospects of **quality of life** by equipping individuals with necessary **skills** (e.g. Reliance Foundation Skilling Academy); b) work towards incorporation of **ecological sustainability** in development activities (e.g. adoption of green belts by DLF Foundation). 4. a) Support **rural development** through **improvements in agriculture (**e.g. National Agro Foundation**);** b) facilitate the mobilization of funds for **electoral politics** (electoral trusts); c) **inspire** a general **culture of philanthropy and volunteerism** among the wider populace (e.g. PM-CARES fund). However, they also face certain **challenges** which are as follows: 1. a) **Regulatory complexities** and compliance burdens (IT Act, FCRA) often constrain operational efficiency; b) **geographical concentration** of trusts in urban and economically advanced regions exacerbates **development disparities**; c) **limited transparency** and inadequate accountability mechanisms in some trusts **undermine public trust** in the sector. 2. a) **Donor-driven agendas** may sometimes overshadow **community needs** and priorities; b) **fragmented approaches** without coordination among trusts lead to **duplication of efforts**; c) **sustainability concerns** arise from **dependence** on individual philanthropists or corporate funding cycles. For public charitable trusts to **maximize their contribution** to inclusive development, **streamlining regulatory** **frameworks**, establishing **collaborative platforms** for coordinated action, and developing **robust impact** **measurement** systems are essential to ensure benefits reach all segments of society. ***(373 words)*** **Additional resources** India’s rich are more willing to give: How philanthropy can tilt scales towards a more equitable society | The Indian Express

questions.questionText: Can the vicious cycle of gender inequality, poverty and malnutrition be broken through microfinancing  of women SHGs? Explain with examples.
questions.subject: Polity

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by defining microfinance.
• In the body, first highlight the potential of microfinancing of women SHGs in breaking the vicious cycle of gender inequality, poverty and malnutrition.
• Next, underline its limitations in this regard.
• Conclude by identifying the need for the structural reform measures to supplement microfinancing. | | --- | According to the **World Bank, microfinance** is the provision of **financial services** to households (low-income, self-employed or informally employed individuals) and micro-enterprises that are **excluded from traditional** **commercial banking services**. Microfinancing of women SHGs can be an effective tool for **addressing gender inequality, poverty and** **malnutrition** in the following ways: 1. a) Easy and affordable **access to capital** (collateral-free loans**)** allows women to engage in **income** **generating avenues** and come out of **inter-generational poverty,** e.g. SEWA Bank, NABARD’s SHG- BLP (Bank Linkage Programme)**;** b) when women contribute financially, they gain respect and **decision-** **making** power within their families and communities, **reducing gender inequality**. 2. a) SHG platforms serve as effective channels for **nutrition education** and **awareness campaigns** e.g., JEEViKA program (Bihar) incorporated nutrition messaging during SHG meetings; b) facilitates **dietary** **diversification** for families through support for **livestock rearing, horticulture** etc. This raises their nutrient intake, helping tackle **malnutrition**. 3. a) Microfinancing of women SHGs **empowers them** to undertake **poverty alleviation programmes,** **influence policies** and raise awareness about social issues like dowry, alcoholism, etc.; b) enable women to advocate for their rights and access public services **(political empowerment)** as many women SHGs work in coordination with Panchayats, e.g. Kudumbashree Model of Kerala. However, microfinance faces the following **limitations i**n this regard: 1. a) Inadequate **financial and business literacy** among members of women SHGs leading to **business** **failures**; b) limited **profit margins** form the activities undertaken by SHGs, which are generally t**raditional and low-scale**. This can potentially lead to **debt traps and crises** in the microfinance sector (e.g. Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis 2010). 2. a) **No direct co-relation** found to exist between increased incomes and improved nutritional outcomes (NFHS-5); b) **limited market access** in remote areas restricts **income-generating opportunities** despite credit availability. 3. a) Limited impact of increased earnings on **entrenched patriarchal attitudes**, possibly resulting in **double-burden** on women; b) can **divert focus** from **macro-scale solutions** (social safety, public health, universal education). To break the **gender-poverty-malnutrition cycle** effectively, SHG microfinancing must be paired with targeted **nutrition training**, **market linkages**, and **gender transformative** approaches. Implementation should prioritize **graduated income support** and measurable **nutrition outcomes** rather than credit alone. (***383 words***) **SEWA**: Self Employed Women's Association; **NABARD**: National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development; **NFHS**: National Family Health Survey **Additional resources** Women self-help groups: Funding alone does not work; the government needs to listen in-ForumIAS Blog Self Help Groups can help in widening women’s labour force participation: Economic Survey 2022-23 - The Hindu

questions.questionText: ‘The West is fostering India as an alternative to reduce dependence on China's supply chain and as a  strategic ally to counter China's political and economic dominance.’ Explain this statement with examples.
questions.subject: International Relations

answers.answerText:
| **Approach:** • Introduce the answer by highlighting the role of recent events in shifting Western focus towards India.
• In the body, first point out the steps taken to reduce the West’s dependence on China’s supply chain, followed by those taken to counter China’s political and economic dominance.
• Conclude by outlining the steps India can take to leverage this shifting preference. | | --- | The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the **West’s over-reliance on China for critical resources**. Also, the Russia- Ukraine conflict highlighted the alignment of **nations hostile to Western interests (**Russia-China-North Korea- Iran**)**. These events have positioned **India as a crucial player** in maintaining global power balance and countering China’s rising influence. The West is fostering India as **an alternative** to China in the following ways: 1. a) **China Plus One Strategy** encourages companies to diversify manufacturing locations due to **rising** **labor costs** in China, **trade tensions**, and the need for **supply chain resilience** b) shift to India due to its **large workforce** and growing **manufacturing capabilities** (e.g. over ₹1.5 trillion worth of iPhones exported from India in FY 2024- 25). 2. a) **Technological collaboration** through initiatives like the Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technologies **(iCET)** b) **India’s domestic policies** are also aiding in diversifying supply chains and reducing reliance on Chinese manufacturing. (e.g. PLI, Make in India). 3. a) **Friendshoring** - relocating supply chains to **political and economic allies** like India with shared values b) Build Back Better World **(B3W) Initiative** launched by G7 as an alternative to China's Belt and Road Initiative **(BRI)** c) India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor **(IMEC)** reducing reliance on Chinese routes and fostering economic ties. **4.** a) Indo-Pacific Economic Framework **(IPEF)** focusing on trade, supply chain resilience, clean energy, and fair economy; b) **USA's Indo-Pacific Strategy** strengthening engagement to **counterbalance China's** influence and aggression; c) Formation of **Quad** (US, India, Japan, Australia) ensuring **a free and open** **Indo-Pacific** region. 5. a) Enhanced **defense cooperation** through joint military exercises (Malabar, Konkan, Varuna); b) **Blue Dot** **Network** mobilizing private sector investment as an alternative to China's BRI c) **QUAD's Supply-Chain** **Resilience Initiative** reducing China's dominance in the Indo-Pacific. India should strive to enhance **infrastructure**, boost **financial inclusion**, strengthen **regulatory frameworks**, promote **innovation and skill development**, and adopt high environmental and social governance **(ESG) standards** to solidify its position as a key global economic player and strategic ally. ***(317 words)*** **Additional resources:** India’s national interest demands better China ties. Don't let West influence it India, China at 75 — a time for strategy, not sentiment - The Hindu Christophe Jaffrelot writes: The West, China, a world in flux — and where India stands | The Indian Express
